q: Tooth enamel is mostly hydroxyapatite, Ca<sub>5</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>OH. Which is the K<sub>sp</sub> expression for its dissolution in water?
h: Write the dissolution equation first. Solids are left out, and each ion concentration is raised to its coefficient.
w: Ca5(PO4)3OH(s) ⇌ 5 Ca2+(aq) + 3 PO43−(aq) + OH−(aq), so Ksp = [Ca2+]5[PO43−]3[OH−]. The solid does not appear in the expression. Coefficients become exponents, not multipliers inside the brackets.
x: The solid hydroxyapatite has constant concentration and is left out of every Ksp expression.
Coefficients become exponents. They are not multiplied into the concentrations inside the brackets.
This ignores the coefficients 5 and 3 from the balanced dissolution equation.

q: The first box shows the dissolved ions in a saturated solution of the salt MX<sub>2</sub> in pure water: 2 M<sup>2+</sup> and 4 X<sup>−</sup> (undissolved solid and water not shown). In a second experiment, MX<sub>2</sub> is saturated in a solution that already contains M(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, at the same temperature (NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> not shown). Boxes I–IV show possible dissolved ions; each ion represents the same concentration in every box. Which box could represent this saturated solution?
h: K<sub>sp</sub> = [M<sup>2+</sup>][X<sup>−</sup>]<sup>2</sup> keeps the same value at the same temperature. Compute the ion product for the pure-water box in 'ion units' and compare.
w: In pure water the ion product is (2)(4)2 = 32 in ion units. A saturated solution at the same temperature must give the same product. Box I: (8)(2)2 = 32, so Box I fits: the added M2+ pushes [X−] down (common-ion effect). Box II gives 128, Box III gives 16 and Box IV gives 54.
x: Box II has (8)(4)² = 128 in ion units, four times the Ksp product, so MX₂ would precipitate. Extra M²⁺ must lower [X⁻].
Box III has (4)(2)² = 16 in ion units, only half the Ksp product, so that solution is unsaturated.
Box IV has (6)(3)² = 54 in ion units, more than the Ksp product of 32, so it is supersaturated.

q: The box shows the ions just after solutions of AgNO<sub>3</sub> and Na<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> are mixed: 4 Ag<sup>+</sup>, 4 NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, 3 CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> and 6 Na<sup>+</sup> (water not shown). Silver chromate, Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>, is very insoluble. After the precipitate forms, which ions remain dissolved in significant amounts?
h: Each Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> uses two Ag<sup>+</sup> for every CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>. Which ion runs out first?
w: Four Ag+ can combine with only two CrO42− (2 : 1 ratio), forming 2 Ag2CrO4. That uses up the Ag+ and leaves one CrO42−. The spectator ions Na+ and NO3− stay dissolved, so the solution holds Na+, NO3− and CrO42−.
x: Silver ion is the limiting ion here. Four Ag⁺ need only two CrO₄²⁻, so the Ag⁺ is used up.
Count the ratio again. Two Ag⁺ go with each CrO₄²⁻, so the ions are not used up evenly.
Ag⁺ is used up when the precipitate forms, so it does not remain in a significant amount.

q: In a Mohr titration, Ag<sup>+</sup> is added slowly to a solution that is 0.010 M Cl<sup>−</sup> and 0.010 M CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>. AgCl forms first, and red Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> marks the end point. Using the K<sub>sp</sub> values in the table, what is [Cl<sup>−</sup>] remaining at the moment Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> begins to precipitate? (Ignore volume change.)
h: Find the [Ag<sup>+</sup>] needed to start Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>; then use that [Ag<sup>+</sup>] in the AgCl K<sub>sp</sub> expression.
w: Ag2CrO4 begins when [Ag+]2(0.010) = 1.1×10−12, so [Ag+] = 1.0×10−5 M. At that [Ag+], [Cl−] = 1.8×10−10 / 1.0×10−5 = 1.7×10−5 M, so over 99.8% of the chloride has already precipitated. 1.0×10−5 M is [Ag+], not [Cl−].
x: 1.8×10⁻⁸ M is the Ag⁺ concentration at which AgCl first appears, not the chloride left later.
1.0×10⁻⁵ M is the Ag⁺ concentration when silver chromate starts. Use it in the AgCl Ksp to find chloride.
AgCl has been precipitating the whole time, so the chloride concentration has fallen far below its starting value.

q: Using the K<sub>sp</sub> values in the table, rank the three salts from LOWEST to HIGHEST molar solubility in pure water.
h: Ksp values compare solubility directly only for salts with the same ion ratio. Solve for s for each: s<sup>2</sup>, 4s<sup>3</sup> and 108s<sup>5</sup>.
w: BaCrO4: s = √(1.2×10−10) = 1.1×10−5 M. Ag2CO3: 4s3 = 8.5×10−12, s = 1.3×10−4 M. Ca3(PO4)2: 108s5 = 2.0×10−29, s = 7.1×10−7 M. So III < I < II. Ranking by Ksp alone would wrongly put BaCrO4 above Ag2CO3.
x: This follows the Ksp values, but the salts have different ion ratios. Solve for s for each salt.
Smaller Ksp does not mean larger solubility. Calcium phosphate has the tiniest solubility of the three.
Silver carbonate is the most soluble of the three once s is calculated from 4s³.

q: Lanthanum iodate dissolves as shown, with K<sub>sp</sub> = 7.5×10<sup>−12</sup> at 25 °C. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
h: If s mol/L dissolves, [La<sup>3+</sup>] = s and [IO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>] = 3s.
w: Ksp = (s)(3s)3 = 27s4 = 7.5×10−12, so s4 = 2.8×10−13 and s = 7.3×10−4 M. Taking a square root treats the salt as 1 : 1, and the fourth root of Ksp alone drops the factor 27.
x: A square root fits a 1:1 salt. Here three iodate ions form per formula unit.
This takes the fourth root of Ksp but leaves out the 3³ = 27 that comes from [IO₃⁻] = 3s.
Writing [IO₃⁻] = 3s means the factor is cubed, giving 27, not 3.

q:
The curve shows all combinations of [M+] and [X−] for which a solution of the salt MX is exactly saturated at 25 °C (Ksp = 4.0×10−10). Points A, B and C are three solutions. Which statements are true?
I. Solution A is unsaturated, so more solid MX could dissolve in it.
II. Adding solid MX to solution B raises both [M+] and [X−].
III. In solution C, MX precipitates until the ion concentrations reach a point on the curve.
h: Compare Q = [M<sup>+</sup>][X<sup>−</sup>] at each point with K<sub>sp</sub>. Points on the curve have Q = K<sub>sp</sub>.
w: I is true: at A, Q = (1.0)(1.5)×10−10 = 1.5×10−10 < Ksp, so A is unsaturated. II is false: B lies on the curve (Q = 4.0×10−10), so it is already saturated and added solid just sits on the bottom. III is true: at C, Q = 1.2×10−9 > Ksp, so solid forms until Q falls to Ksp. The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true. At C, Q is greater than Ksp, so the solution is supersaturated and solid MX forms.
Statement I is true and statement II is false. A is below the curve (unsaturated), while B is already saturated.
Statement II is false. B lies on the curve, so it is already saturated and extra solid does not dissolve.

q: Silver bromide dissolves in aqueous ammonia because Ag<sup>+</sup> forms [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>. Using the constants in the table, what is the molar solubility of AgBr in 1.0 M NH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Add the two equations: AgBr(s) + 2 NH<sub>3</sub> ⇌ [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> + Br<sup>−</sup>. Its K is K<sub>sp</sub> × K<sub>f</sub>.
w: K = (5.0×10−13)(1.7×107) = 8.5×10−6. With s = [complex] = [Br−]: s2/(1.0 − 2s)2 = 8.5×10−6, so s/(1.0 − 2s) = 2.92×10−3 and s = 2.9×10−3 M, about 4000 times its solubility in pure water (7.1×10−7 M).
x: This is the solubility in pure water. The ammonia pulls Ag⁺ into the complex, so far more AgBr dissolves.
This is K for the overall reaction. Molar solubility comes from setting K equal to s²/[NH₃]².
This uses Ksp divided by Kf. Adding the two reactions means the constants are multiplied.

q: Calomel, Hg<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, contains the diatomic mercury(I) ion, Hg<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup>. Its molar solubility in water at 25 °C is 6.5×10<sup>−7</sup> M. What is its K<sub>sp</sub>?
h: Write the dissolution with the Hg<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup> ion kept together: how many ions of each kind form per formula unit?
w: Hg2Cl2(s) ⇌ Hg22+(aq) + 2 Cl−(aq), so Ksp = (s)(2s)2 = 4s3 = 4(6.5×10−7)3 = 1.1×10−18. Splitting the dimer into two Hg+ ions would wrongly give (2s)2(2s)2 = 16s4.
x: This treats mercury(I) as two separate Hg⁺ ions. The Hg₂²⁺ ion stays together in solution.
This multiplies s by s². The chloride concentration is 2s, and that whole quantity is squared.
This doubles s³ instead of squaring the 2 in [Cl⁻] = 2s.

q: Two slightly soluble salts have the same K<sub>sp</sub> at 25 °C, as listed in the table. How do their molar solubilities in pure water compare?
c: NZ<sub>2</sub> is about 50 times more soluble than MY.
They are equally soluble because their K<sub>sp</sub> values are equal.
MY is about 50 times more soluble than NZ<sub>2</sub>.
NZ<sub>2</sub> is about 2 times more soluble than MY.
h: Solve s<sup>2</sup> = K<sub>sp</sub> for MY and 4s<sup>3</sup> = K<sub>sp</sub> for NZ<sub>2</sub>.
w: MY: s = √(4.0×10−12) = 2.0×10−6 M. NZ2: 4s3 = 4.0×10−12, s = 1.0×10−4 M. So NZ2 is about 50 times more soluble. Equal Ksp values mean equal solubility only when the ion ratios match.
x: Equal Ksp gives equal solubility only for salts with the same ion ratio. These two differ.
Check the direction. A cube root of a tiny number is much larger than a square root of a similar number.
The ratio is not just the 2 in the formula. Calculate each s from its own Ksp expression.

q: The box shows all the dissolved ions in a saturated solution of calcium phosphate, Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (undissolved solid and water not shown). Each ion represents 1.0×10<sup>−7</sup> M. What is the molar solubility of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>?
h: Molar solubility counts formula units dissolved. How many Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> units would release these ions?
w: The box has 6 Ca2+ and 4 PO43−. Each formula unit gives 3 Ca2+ and 2 PO43−, so 2 formula units dissolved: s = 2 × 1.0×10−7 M = 2.0×10−7 M. 6.0×10−7 M is [Ca2+] and 4.0×10−7 M is [PO43−].
x: This counts every ion. Molar solubility counts the formula units that dissolved.
This is the calcium ion concentration. Each formula unit releases three Ca²⁺.
This is the phosphate ion concentration. Each formula unit releases two PO₄³⁻.

q: The graph shows log(molar solubility) of a metal hydroxide M(OH)<sub>2</sub> in buffered solutions at 25 °C. What is K<sub>sp</sub> of M(OH)<sub>2</sub>?
h: Read one point, such as pH 10.00. In a buffer, [OH<sup>−</sup>] is set by the pH, and [M<sup>2+</sup>] equals the molar solubility.
w: At pH 10.00, log s = −3.0, so [M2+] = 1.0×10−3 M, and pOH = 4.00 gives [OH−] = 1.0×10−4 M. Ksp = (1.0×10−3)(1.0×10−4)2 = 1.0×10−11. Every point gives the same value, and the slope of −2 reflects the two OH− in the formula.
x: This leaves [OH⁻] unsquared. The formula has two hydroxide ions.
This uses [OH⁻] = 2s as if the salt were in pure water. In a buffer the pH fixes [OH⁻].
This uses [H⁺] instead of [OH⁻]. Convert the pH to pOH first.

q: Acid rain dissolves limestone by the overall reaction shown. Using the constants in the table, what is K for this reaction?
h: Combine the dissolution of CaCO<sub>3</sub> with the reverse of the HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ionization (CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> → HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O).
w: CaCO3(s) ⇌ Ca2+ + CO32− has K = Ksp. CO32− + H3O+ ⇌ HCO3− + H2O is the reverse of the Ka2 reaction, so K = 1/Ka2. Adding them: K = Ksp/Ka2 = 4.5×10−9 / 4.7×10−11 = 96. K > 1 shows why acid dissolves carbonate rock.
x: This multiplies Ksp by Ka2. The ionization step is reversed, so its constant is inverted.
This is Ka2 divided by Ksp, the reciprocal of the right combination.
This is Ksp alone. Reaction with H₃O⁺ removes carbonate, which also enters K.

q: Potassium chromate is added slowly to a solution that is 0.010 M in both Pb<sup>2+</sup> and Ag<sup>+</sup>. Using the K<sub>sp</sub> values in the table, which solid forms first, and at what [CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>] does it begin to form?
h: For each salt, solve K<sub>sp</sub> = Q for the [CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>] needed. The salt needing less chromate forms first.
w: PbCrO4: [CrO42−] = 2.8×10−13/0.010 = 2.8×10−11 M. Ag2CrO4: [CrO42−] = 1.1×10−12/(0.010)2 = 1.1×10−8 M. Far less chromate is needed for lead, so PbCrO4 forms first, at 2.8×10−11 M.
x: This forgets to square [Ag⁺]. Even so, the value is larger than the lead chromate threshold.
This is the right threshold for silver chromate, but lead chromate needs far less chromate and forms first.
This is the Ksp itself. Divide by [Pb²⁺] to find the chromate concentration needed.

q: NaOH(aq) is added drop by drop to Zn(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>(aq). A white precipitate forms, and with excess NaOH it dissolves again. Which equations, in order, describe these two observations?
h: Zinc hydroxide is amphoteric. What does it do with a large excess of hydroxide ion?
w: First Zn2+ and OH− form the precipitate (equation I). With excess OH−, Zn(OH)2 acts as an acid and forms the soluble complex ion [Zn(OH)4]2− (equation II), so I, then II. Equation III needs added acid, not base.
x: Equation III uses H₃O⁺. Only base is being added here.
The precipitate must form before it can dissolve, so equation II cannot come first.
Equation III needs acid. In excess base the hydroxide forms a complex ion instead.
